ai_summary: Great Britain’s wind output currently registers at 13.6 GW, heavily underpinned by an estimated Scottish wind output of 5.0 GW, which represents 49.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust volume of local green generation has driven Scottish carbon intensity down to an exceptional 1 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide carbon intensity of 122 gCO2/kWh. However, persistent cross-border transmission limits prevent the full evacuation of this clean electricity to major demand centers across Great Britain. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today stands at 44.7 GWh, resulting in an operational constraint cost of about £1,135,763. To compensate for this stranded power and maintain system stability, an estimated 8,491,157 m3 of gas was burned elsewhere on the network. This thermal substitution added 15,642 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere, working directly against broader decarbonisation objectives. These metrics highlight the acute operational trade-offs currently facing the energy system, where surplus low-carbon generation in Scotland coexists with high consumer balancing costs and avoidable fossil-fuel emissions elsewhere on the national grid.
